summary: This informational document specifies two encryption types and two checksum types for Kerberos 5. The new types use AES in CTS mode for confidentiality and HMAC with a SHA-2 hash for integrity.

eli5.summary: Kerberos is a login system using secret codes. This adds two newer ways of scrambling messages and checking nobody changed them.

subtitle: Modern encryption and integrity protection for Kerberos network authentication.

tldr.problem: Kerberos needed encryption and checksums that keep pace with modern cryptographic standards, using stronger algorithms and better key derivation practices.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8009 specifies two encryption types (aes128-cts-hmac-sha256-128 and aes256-cts-hmac-sha384-192) that combine AES in CTS mode for confidentiality with HMAC-SHA-2 for integrity, derived using PBKDF2 and a specialized key derivation function.
tldr.outcome: These encryption types are now standard options in Kerberos 5 implementations, replacing older AES variants with stronger cryptographic guarantees and better resistance to password attacks.

today: RFC 8009 remains the standard specification for these encryption types in Kerberos 5. It is informational (not standards-track) but describes the encryption methods that are now widely deployed in modern Kerberos implementations.

sections.title: Introduction to AES-SHA2 for Kerberos
sections.content:
RFC 8009 defines two new encryption types and two new checksum types for Kerberos 5. These types use AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) in CTS mode (ciphertext stealing) for encrypting data, and HMAC-SHA-2 (HMAC with SHA-256 or SHA-384) for verifying that messages have not been modified.

The core improvement over the previous AES types in RFC 3962 is that these new types follow modern cryptographic best practices: the HMAC is computed over the ciphertext instead of the plaintext, which lets the receiver verify integrity before decryption, and the key derivation process uses NIST-recommended functions that are more resistant to password-guessing attacks.
sections.eli5: Think of it like sealing a letter: the old way sealed the envelope without checking the seal was real. This new way checks the seal first before opening, and uses a better lock that is harder to guess.

sections.title: Message Format and Encryption Process
sections.content:
When encrypting a message, the system prepends a 16-byte random confounder to the plaintext. This random value serves the purpose of an initialization vector. The plaintext (confounder plus actual data) is then encrypted using AES in CBC-CS3 mode, also called ciphertext stealing mode, which avoids expanding the ciphertext beyond the plaintext length.

After encryption, the system computes an HMAC of the cipher state concatenated with the ciphertext output. For aes128-cts-hmac-sha256-128, this HMAC is truncated to 128 bits; for aes256-cts-hmac-sha384-192, it is truncated to 192 bits. The final ciphertext is the encrypted output plus the truncated HMAC.

Decryption reverses this: the receiver removes and verifies the HMAC against the cipher state and ciphertext, then decrypts only if the HMAC is correct, and finally discards the confounder to recover the original message.
sections.eli5: The sender scrambles the message and adds a tamper-evident seal. The receiver checks the seal is real before opening, and throws away a random part the sender added at the start.

sections.title: Key Derivation and Generation
sections.content:
The system maintains three keys per encryption operation: Kc (checksum key), Ke (encryption key), and Ki (integrity key). These are derived from a single base-key using the KDF-HMAC-SHA2 function defined in the RFC, following NIST Special Publication 800-108.

When deriving keys from a user passphrase, the system uses PBKDF2 (Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2) with a salt value and a default iteration count of 32,768. The salt is constructed by concatenating the encryption type name, a null byte, and a realm-specific salt string. This process produces a base-key, which is then fed into KDF-HMAC-SHA2 to produce the three working keys.

For aes128-cts-hmac-sha256-128, HMAC-SHA-256 is used for key derivation; for aes256-cts-hmac-sha384-192, HMAC-SHA-384 is used. The use of unique salts and high iteration counts significantly increases resistance to offline dictionary attacks and rainbow table attacks.
sections.eli5: To turn a password into a secret key, the system grinds it many times (32,768 times) with a unique mix-in value, making guessing the key impossibly slow. Then it cuts the result into three smaller secret pieces.

sections.title: Security Characteristics and Trade-offs
sections.content:
The encryption types achieve a balanced security profile by pairing key sizes and hash outputs: aes128-cts-hmac-sha256-128 uses a 128-bit AES key and SHA-256 (truncated to 128 bits for integrity) for a uniform 128-bit security level. aes256-cts-hmac-sha384-192 uses a 256-bit AES key and SHA-384 (truncated to 192 bits) for a uniform 192-bit security level, with SHA-384 matched to AES-256 rather than AES-192 to leverage efficient hardware implementations.

The specification addresses several security concerns. Random number generation quality is critical, and implementers should use approved cryptographic random generators. For cross-realm authentication (where two different Kerberos realms trust each other), the specification notes that the enctype name is prepended to the salt; this ensures that different encryption types produce different keys from the same passphrase, preventing accidental key reuse. The specification also acknowledges that some implementations may use fixed salts or administrator-shared passwords for cross-realm services, which can limit the effectiveness of salt-based protections.
sections.eli5: This design makes it hard to break by guessing: a good random source is essential, and the recipe for turning a password into a key is carefully engineered to match modern math.

sections.title: Status and Implementation
sections.content:
IANA has assigned encryption type numbers 19 and 20 for aes128-cts-hmac-sha256-128 and aes256-cts-hmac-sha384-192 respectively. The corresponding checksum types are assigned numbers 19 and 20 as well.

RFC 8009 is informational and describes what many Kerberos implementations have already adopted. The document includes extensive test vectors in Appendix A for verification of implementations, covering key derivation, encryption with various plaintext sizes, checksum computation, and pseudorandom function outputs. These test vectors are essential for ensuring interoperability across different implementations and platforms.

The specification does not obsolete RFC 3962, which remains in use. Both sets of encryption types coexist in the Kerberos ecosystem, with newer implementations preferring the SHA-2 variants for their stronger cryptographic foundations.
sections.eli5: These encryption methods are now a standard choice in Kerberos, with test cases provided so every implementation does the math the same way.

data.title: Message with Confounder, Encryption, and HMAC

fields.name: Confounder
fields.desc: 16-byte random value; acts as initialization vector.

fields.name: Ciphertext
fields.desc: Encrypted confounder and plaintext via AES CTS mode.

fields.name: HMAC
fields.desc: 128 or 192 bits; truncated HMAC-SHA-2 of cipher state plus ciphertext.

items.title: Kc (Checksum Key)
items.text: Derived from base-key; used by HMAC for standalone checksums.

items.title: Ke (Encryption Key)
items.text: Derived from base-key; used to encrypt and decrypt messages with AES.

items.title: Ki (Integrity Key)
items.text: Derived from base-key; used to compute authenticated encryption HMAC.
